Fascism. An authoritarian political ideology that emerged in early twentieth-century Europe, fascism was characterized by extreme nationalism, militarism, hierarchical social organization, and centralized state control under a charismatic leader. It rejected democracy and liberalism, embraced violence and propaganda, and achieved power in Italy under Benito Mussolini and in Germany under Adolf Hitler, resulting in some of history's most destructive regimes.

Fascism originated in the early nineteen-twenties in Italy. Mussolini blended nationalist fervor, syndicalist corporatism, and authoritarian hierarchy, claiming to transcend both capitalism and communism through organic national unity. Key fascist characteristics included extreme nationalism, sometimes grounded in racial pseudoscience, militarism, a cult of personality around the leader, suppression of opposition, corporatist economic organization, and rejection of democratic values and individual rights.

Nazi Germany adapted fascism to include antisemitism and racial pseudoscience, producing the most destructive fascist regime. The Nazis merged fascism with racial ideology and launched World War II. Fascism appealed to insecure middle classes frightened by economic crisis, national humiliation, or social instability, as seen across post-World War One Europe.

Fascist movements used mass propaganda, spectacle, and violence through paramilitary street gangs to consolidate power and suppress opposition. They controlled media and employed tactics that would influence later authoritarian movements. Despite their opposition to communism, which attracted business elites and conservative politicians initially, fascist regimes ultimately subordinated capitalism entirely to state control, revealing their true radicalism.

Fascism is now widely viewed as morally and politically repugnant. Postwar democracies adopted constitutional protections against fascist movements, though fascistic tendencies periodically reemerge in political discourse, reminding us that authoritarianism remains a persistent human temptation.
